PRIMAL RELIGIONS - THE TRADITIONS OF EARLY PEOPLES - STUDY NOTES

OPENING QUOTE
- Book of Job: 'Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?'
- This quote points to the mystery of God that early peoples tried to reach.

WHAT ARE PRIMAL RELIGIONS?
- Primal religions: the religious traditions of early peoples. All religions are rooted in them.
- They date back to 50,000 BCE.
- Early peoples were an agricultural people who lived close to nature.
- They sensed the powers of nature and were at the mercy of natural disasters: storms, floods, disease and famine.
- Their traditions were linked to real human needs.
- Their traditions were the outward expression of a belief in a spiritual world of powers or beings stronger than humans.
- Thousands of distinct indigenous (native) religious traditions were practised in the ancient world.

EXAMPLES OF PRIMAL / ANCIENT RELIGIONS
- The Sumerians: ancient Near East, in Mesopotamia. Built ziggurat temples (pyramid-shaped towers) dedicated to various deities.
- The Maya: Central and South America. Their sacred calendars linked days to deities.
- Ancient religions of Africa: focused on directing the living towards harmony with the spirit world (see chapter 9 on African religion).
- The Maori of New Zealand: placed great emphasis on land and other sacred locations. Each person and everything was understood to have an essence called 'mauri'.

WHY THESE RELIGIONS ARE GROUPED TOGETHER - THREE SHARED FEATURES
- a) They recognise the all-encompassing power of religion. There are no boundaries between sacred and secular - religion is part of all of life.
- b) They use oral (spoken) rather than written sources and traditions.
- c) They act out traditional stories or myths in rituals. These rituals expressed: the nature of the relationship between humans and the divine; community living; the centrality of the natural world to all life.
- This imitative behaviour (acting out the myths) helped people memorise the oral traditions.

VARIETY IN PRIMAL RELIGION
- There is huge variety in belief and practice - an 'elaborate tapestry'.
- Archaeological and historical research has found some common themes.
- But day-to-day living out of beliefs led to rituals and practices unique to each indigenous group.

ARCHAEOLOGICAL EVIDENCE - FOUR GROUPINGS
- Burial places and finds.
- Offerings and sacrifices.
- Representations of deities - paintings, carvings, etc.
- Religious constructions - temples, altars, etc.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE TELLS US
- Burial: our ancient ancestors took great care over the rituals of death. This suggests a belief in some form of afterlife.
- Offerings and sacrifices: show a strong belief in spirits and a desire to appease, praise, beg or honour deities linked to different parts of life and the cycle of the seasons.
- The central belief in a spirit world, and the acting out of ritual in word, symbol and sacred space, all find echoes in religion today.

WHAT EARLY PEOPLE TEACH US
- They show the importance of trying to penetrate (get into) the mystery of life.
- Their dependence on nature led to beliefs that certain gods controlled specific parts of nature - rain, crops, thunder and so on.
- Shamans developed sacrifices, rituals and charms to appease the gods, to protect, and to produce needed food.
- This shows the sense of wonder and awe common to all people in every age and civilisation.
- The scope and immensity of the universe still challenges our understanding and inspires our sense of mystery.
- Reaching out to what is above and beyond worldly things, to touch the mystery and open up to the holy, is a human response to this experience.

WHAT RELIGIONS DO FOR PEOPLE
- Religions cater for all types of human need.
- They answer questions and provide challenges.
- They offer answers to the different levels of the search for meaning.
- They give encouragement, inspiration and comfort.
- They provide a way of being fully human, living in fellowship and community as we try to create a better world.

KEY CONCEPTS OF PRIMAL RELIGIONS

MANA
- Mana: power embedded in an object or person. Origin: Melanesian.
- The power of mana comes from kinship (family connection) with gods and ancestors.
- Some people, places or things have more mana than others - they are more gifted and powerful.
- Example: tribal chiefs embody the mana of their people and land.
- Mana is an impersonal force. It is the manifestation (showing) of the spirit world.
- Encounters between different kinds and strengths of mana are tense, even dangerous.
- To manage these encounters, social restrictions and boundaries are marked off - these are called tabu (taboo).

TABU (TABOO)
- Tabu: any person, object or place 'set apart', removed from everyday use and consecrated for ritual and worship. Origin: Polynesian.
- Rules of tabu preserve the power and sacredness of mana.
- Tabu things channel the mana of the spirit world.
- Sacred places and objects - e.g. vessels, instruments, symbols, dance masks, head-dresses - can only be used by mana-filled people who are ritually consecrated and pure.
- Rules of ablution (washing), purification, touch, gesture and sound keep the 'otherness' or 'separateness' of what is tabu.
- Breaking these rules requires reparation (making amends) or sacrifice, to avoid the punishment of illness.

TOTEM
- Totem: something natural (usually an animal, bird or plant) that symbolises the spiritual essence of a person or group and connects them with their spiritual ancestry.
- The word comes from the Ojibwa people of Canada: 'dotem/oteman' meaning 'the person is a relative of mine'.
- For North American Indians and Australian Aborigines, totems had deep and special significance.
- Worship practices showing the sacredness of the totem often arose from the tribe's awe and respect for nature and the environment, on which they relied for survival.

SHAMAN
- Shaman: a tribal elder or holy person who is a living mediator between the human world and the spirit world.
- Shamanism is a feature of many primal traditions. It originated with the Tungus people of Siberia and north-east China.
- The shaman usually inherited the gift from his or her ancestors.
- He or she builds a close relationship with a spiritual guardian through fasting and prayer.
- The shaman makes journeys into the spirit world to gain prophetic wisdom and knowledge of (often herbal) medicine, to give physical and spiritual healing.
- Uses magic and divination to influence and control spirits who affect nature and human affairs.
- Sacred trances are often the medium for contact with the spirit world.
- Uses special charms, chants and sacrifices to interpret the will of the gods and cure disease.
- Activities range from: knowing the movements of fish shoals; healing with sacred sand paintings; interpreting dreams.
- The shaman is 'seized by the Divine' - controlling the spirits yet possessed by them.
- Today more and more people still look to shamans for advice and counselling.

PEOPLES WHO PRACTISED ANCIENT RELIGIONS (list for project work)
- Sumerians, Babylonians, Assyrians, Canaanites, Ancient Egyptians, Celts, Maya, Aztecs, Incas.
- Ancient Africans, e.g. the Yoruba of Nigeria, the Dozon of Mali, the Bwiti of Gabon.
- Maori, Aborigines, Oceanians, Native Americans, Amazonians.

KEY TERMS
- Mana: power in a person or object, from kinship with gods and ancestors (Melanesian).
- Tabu: set apart and consecrated for ritual; rules that protect mana (Polynesian).
- Totem: a natural symbol (animal, bird, plant) of a group's spiritual essence and ancestry (Ojibwa).
- Shaman: holy person who mediates between the human and spirit worlds (Tungus).

rows.prompt: Explain the concept of a totem.

rows.prompt: Describe the role of a shaman.
rows.model_answer: A shaman is a tribal elder or holy person who mediates between the human world and the spirit world. Through fasting, prayer and sacred trances, the shaman journeys into the spirit world to gain wisdom and healing knowledge. Shamans use charms, chants, sacrifices, magic and divination to heal, interpret dreams and know the will of the gods.

rows.prompt: Explain any two of the following concepts associated with primal religion: (a) Mana (b) Tabu (c) Totem (d) Shaman.
rows.model_answer: Mana is a concept of Melanesian origin. It refers to power embedded in a person or object, which comes from kinship with the gods and ancestors. Some people, places and things have more mana than others; for example, tribal chiefs embody the mana of their people and land. Mana is an impersonal force that shows the spirit world. Because meetings between different strengths of mana are tense and dangerous, boundaries called tabu are marked off. A shaman is found in many primal traditions and the idea comes from the Tungus people of Siberia and north-east China. The shaman is usually a tribal elder or holy person who inherited the gift from ancestors and acts as a living mediator between the human world and the spirit world. Through fasting and prayer the shaman builds a relationship with a spiritual guardian. In sacred trances he or she journeys into the spirit world to gain prophetic wisdom and knowledge of herbal medicine, and uses charms, chants and sacrifices to heal disease and interpret the will of the gods. The shaman is 'seized by the Divine', controlling spirits yet possessed by them.

rows.prompt: Discuss what archaeological evidence reveals about the religious beliefs of early peoples.
rows.model_answer: Primal religions date back to 50,000 BCE, and because they used oral rather than written traditions, much of what we know comes from archaeology. The evidence falls into four groupings: burial places and finds; offerings and sacrifices; representations of deities such as paintings and carvings; and religious constructions such as temples and altars. Burial evidence shows our ancestors took great care over rituals of death, which suggests a belief in some form of afterlife. Offerings and sacrifices show a strong belief in spirits and a desire to appease, praise, beg or honour gods connected with different areas of life and the cycle of the seasons. Because early peoples were agricultural and depended on nature, they believed certain gods controlled rain, crops and thunder. Religious constructions like the Sumerian ziggurats, pyramid-shaped towers in Mesopotamia, show the importance of sacred space. While research reveals common themes, it also shows great variety, with rituals unique to each group. Above all the evidence shows a sense of wonder and awe and an effort to penetrate the mystery of life, which still echoes in religion today.

rows.prompt: Outline the main characteristics shared by primal religions, using examples from at least two ancient peoples.
rows.model_answer: Primal religions are the traditions of early agricultural peoples who lived close to nature and were at the mercy of storms, floods, disease and famine. Their traditions expressed belief in a spiritual world of beings stronger than humans. They are grouped together for three reasons. First, religion was all-encompassing, with no boundary between sacred and secular. Second, they relied on oral rather than written traditions. Third, they acted out myths in rituals that expressed the human-divine relationship, community life and the centrality of nature; this imitation helped people memorise their traditions. Examples show this. The Sumerians of Mesopotamia built ziggurat temples to their gods. The Maya of Central and South America had sacred calendars linking days to deities. Ancient African religions aimed to bring the living into harmony with the spirit world. The Maori of New Zealand stressed land and sacred places and believed every person and thing had an essence, mauri. Despite these shared features, there was huge variety, with each group developing its own rituals.

rows.prompt: 'Early people show us the importance of trying to penetrate the mystery of life.' Discuss this statement.
rows.model_answer: Early peoples depended completely on nature and were exposed to storms, floods, disease and famine. Faced with this, they sensed powers greater than themselves and believed certain gods controlled parts of nature such as rain, crops and thunder. Shamans developed sacrifices, rituals and charms to appease the gods, to protect the community and to produce needed food. Their careful burials show they reflected on death and the afterlife, and their offerings show a desire to praise, beg or honour the gods through the cycle of the seasons. All of this reveals a sense of wonder and awe common to people in every age. Today the size of the universe still challenges our understanding and inspires mystery. Reaching out to what is beyond the world, to touch the mystery and open up to the holy, is a basic human response. Like early peoples, religions today answer deep questions, give comfort and inspiration and help people live fully human lives in community.
